title: Text Has Curvature
claim: A local object, evidence of non-flatness, a signed curvature definition and downstream control uses fit together as one framework.
layout: 2x2 panels with captions, reading left-to-right then down, color-coded blue/orange
description: A 2x2 grid of panels, each with its own caption below. (a) A prefix box and a suffix box point at a '?' slot. Below it, a blue left-belief bar chart and an orange right-belief bar chart are linked by dashed arrows, under the question 'How do μL and μR compose?'. (b) Two columns, 'Order matters' and 'Evidence interacts'. The first shows two arrow chains that apply prefix and suffix in opposite orders and end in different belief histograms, marked ≠. The second shows μL × μR ≠ the observed belief, drawn in green. (c) Two triangle sketches. Focus is blue, with directions that converge. Fan-out is orange, with directions that diverge from a slot. (d) A token row shaded green, gray or orange, with a κ bar chart below it. A legend marks kept, pruned and fan-out (retrieve) tokens. Blue and orange carry meaning throughout. The eye starts at the top-left slot and ends at the bar chart.
caption: Texture overview. (a) Our primitive object is a two-sided slot with prefix/suffix beliefs. (b) Natural text exhibits non-flat two-sided belief composition (order-sensitivity and evidence interaction), motivating curvature and enabling definition-independent existence tests (Section [ref]). (c) Texture defines a text-native signed curvature from how the two-sided belief field contracts (focus) or expands (fan-out) under a neutral semantic transport geometry (Section [ref]). (d) The resulting curvature field is a general-purpose control signal: we instantiate it on pruning and retrieval, but it applies broadly to language tasks requiring context-aware resource allocation (Section [ref]).
abstract: Does natural language text have an intrinsic curvature? Language is increasingly modeled in curved geometries - hyperbolic spaces for hierarchy, mixed-curvature manifolds for compositional structure - yet a basic scientific question remains unresolved: what does curvature mean for text itself, in a way that is native to language rather than an artifact of the embedding space we choose? We argue that text does indeed have curvature, and show how to detect it, define it, and use it. To this end, we propose Texture, a text-native, word-level discrete curvature signal, and make three contributions. (a) Existence: We provide empirical and theoretical certificates that semantic inference in natural corpora is non-flat. (b) Definition: We define Texture as a signed two-axis curvature of the word-in-context belief field - the differential of reconciliation between prefix and suffix - measuring, via a debiased SchrÃ¶dinger transport divergence, whether adding context from one side contracts the semantic effect of context from the other side (focus, positive) or expands it into competing continuations (fan-out, negative). (c) Utility: Texture is actionable: it serves as a general-purpose measurement and control primitive enabling geometry without geometric training; we instantiate it on two representative tasks, improving long-context inference through curvature-guided compression and retrieval-augmented generation through curvature-guided routing. Together, our results establish a text-native curvature paradigm, making Texture practically useful.
